text: raw_customers only ever shows a customer's current status. If leadership asks which customers churned last quarter, a table holding only today's value has no way to answer that — the history is already gone.
A dbt snapshot solves this with real, standard syntax: a snapshot block, configured with a target schema, a unique key, and the timestamp strategy comparing an updated_at column.

Strategy timestamp compares each row's updated_at against what's already recorded, inserting a new row whenever it moved forward. unique_key ties those rows to the same real customer, and dbt adds its own valid_from and valid_to columns automatically.

Running dbt snapshot checks every row against what's already recorded. A customer whose status just changed gets a brand-new snapshot row — and querying by customer id with those valid_from and valid_to columns reconstructs their real status history.

A snapshot is itself a governance artifact — the platform's version-controlled answer to whether history can be reconstructed. Next: a shared macro library, so business rules like this don't get redefined inconsistently across models.
